choices.text: An inward, centre-seeking push from the seat and door; there is no outward force

questions.feedback: That trap reading is the one to unlearn: A centrifugal force flings you outward in a sharp turn. Reteach point: No outward fling exists: your body wants to keep going straight while the seat pushes you inward - the inward push is the real force.
questions.misconception: A centrifugal force flings you outward in a sharp turn.
questions.prompt: In a sharp turn, a passenger feels flung outward. What force actually acts on the passenger horizontally?

questions.answer: F = mv^2/r = 1200 x 225 / 50 = 5400 N, directed toward the centre of the bend (supplied by friction).
questions.feedback: The formula is F = mv^2/r with the direction always to the centre. If you used v instead of v^2 you under-counted - the force grows with the square of the speed.
questions.prompt: A car of mass 1200 kg rounds a bend of radius 50 m at 15 m/s. Calculate the centripetal force needed and state its direction.

questions.feedback: A geostationary satellite must turn at the same rate as the Earth below, so its period is exactly 24 hours, above the equator and in the same direction as the rotation.
questions.prompt: What is the period of a geostationary orbit?

questions.answer: F = GMm/r^2. The gravitational attraction toward the Earth is itself the centripetal force holding the Moon on its circular path.
questions.feedback: For orbits there is no separate centripetal force on top of gravity: gravity IS the centre-seeking force, so GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r for a circular orbit.
questions.prompt: Gravity holds the Moon in orbit. Write down the gravitation law and name the quantity that plays the role of the centripetal force for the Moon.
